items.title: Distraction-Related Phenomena in Emergency Department Work: A Systematic Literature Review from a Cognitive Ergonomics Perspective
items.abstract: Background: Emergency departments are cognitively demanding environments where healthcare professionals are frequently exposed to interruptions and other distracting factors that may compromise workflow and patient safety. This systematic review aimed to identify factors that distract healthcare professionals in emergency departments and to synthesise their cognitive, organisational, and patient-safety consequences from a cognitive ergonomics perspective. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted in PubMed, CINAHL Ultimate, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement. Studies meeting predefined eligibility criteria were included. Methodological quality was assessed using design-specific critical appraisal tools, and findings were synthesised using inductive content analysis. Results: Nineteen studies met the predefined eligibility criteria and were included in the synthesis. The most frequently reported distraction-related phenomena included communication-related interruptions, telephone calls, and technological and environmental disturbances, while multitasking and task switching were identified as related work processes or responses to competing demands. Across the studies, distraction-related phenomena were associated with cognitive and workflow consequences, including increased workload, reduced situation awareness, work-related stress, and workflow disruption. Only one of the 19 included studies directly examined task errors, whereas the others identified interruptions during medication-related activities and potential safety concerns without directly measuring medication errors or patient harm. Several studies also identified clinically relevant interruptions associated with information exchange and care coordination, alongside unnecessary or poorly timed interruptions that were perceived as disruptive. Conclusions: Distraction-related phenomena are common features of emergency department work and are associated with cognitive and workflow outcomes. However, direct evidence regarding clinical errors and patient safety outcomes remains limited, and the available findings do not establish a causal relationship between distraction-related phenomena and patient harm. Potential cognitive-ergonomic strategies may focus on reducing avoidable and low-value interruptions while preserving clinically necessary communication that supports information exchange and care coordination; however, their effectiveness requires empirical evaluation.

items.title: Does transparency matter when interacting with social bots? An experiment on user engagement behaviors in Chinese social media
items.abstract: Purpose While transparency is widely promoted as a principle of responsible AI design, its behavioral consequences remain contested, particularly in Chinese social media contexts. This study examines whether different levels of social bot transparency reduce or facilitate user engagement, and whether these effects depend on users' prior knowledge of social bots. Design/methodology/approach An online experiment was conducted in a simulated Weibo environment. A total of 731 participants were randomly assigned to one of three transparency conditions: low, medium, or high transparency. User engagement behaviors were measured through participants' behavioral choices, including reading, liking/sharing, replying, and combined engagement actions. Multinomial logistic regression and subgroup analyses were used to examine the effects of transparency and the moderating role of prior knowledge. Findings Social bot transparency significantly reduces active user engagement. Compared with high transparency, low transparency increases the likelihood of liking/sharing, replying, and combined reply-based engagement rather than merely reading. Medium transparency produces engagement patterns similar to high transparency, suggesting that even ambiguous bot identity cues may activate non-human attribution and suppress active engagement. Prior knowledge moderates this relationship: users with limited prior knowledge are more sensitive to transparency cues, whereas those with higher prior knowledge show more stable engagement across transparency conditions. Originality/value This study extends social bot transparency research beyond binary disclosure by identifying a categorical identity-attribution mechanism. It also clarifies prior knowledge as a boundary condition of algorithm aversion in human-AI interaction.

items.title: Dual context attentive feature network: an interpretable dual-pathway deep learning framework for accurate gastrointestinal endoscopic image classification
items.abstract: Background: Gastrointestinal (GI) diseases such as colorectal cancer and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) contribute substantially to global morbidity, with colorectal cancer accounting for nearly 10% of all cancer diagnoses worldwide. Many existing artificial intelligence (AI) models suffer from limited generalizability and poor clinical interpretability. This study aimed to develop and evaluate an explainable AI (XAI) framework for classifying GI diseases from endoscopic images. Methods: Public datasets from the Simula Research Laboratory were used: Hyper-Kvasir (10,662 images) for training, Kvasir-V1 (4,000 images) for validation, and Kvasir-V2 (8,000 images) as an independent test set. Two convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, GastroNet-dilated multi-scale attention (DMSA) (a proposed DMSA Network) and M2ShallowNet (a lightweight hybrid model), were designed for complementary feature extraction. Deep features were fused using a dual context attentive feature network (DCAF-Net) followed by Aquila Optimizer (AO)-based feature-weight refinement without introducing additional trainable fusion parameters. Performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, and statistical testing. Interpretability was examined using gradient-weighted class activation mapping++ (Grad-CAM++) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Results: The best-performing classifier, a multilayer perceptron (MLP), achieved an accuracy of 97.21%, precision of 97.27%, recall of 97.21%, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 96.82%, and F1-score of 97.21% on the independent test set. ROC analysis demonstrated excellent class separability, and statistical testing confirmed reliable generalization. XAI results highlighted regions that qualitatively correspond to pathological areas; formal clinical validation of these interpretations was not performed in this study. Conclusions: The proposed framework offers a promising research prototype for AI-assisted GI disease classification. Its potential for real-world endoscopic deployment requires further prospective validation before clinical adoption.

items.title: Dynamics of collective creativity in AI art competitions
items.abstract: Abstract Creativity is a fundamental part of cultural evolution, but the mechanisms by which groups produce novelty are notoriously difficult to infer from the historical record. Iterated learning experiments have shown that cultural transmission reliably distorts artifacts toward the inductive biases of learners, but most of this work uses linear chains of human participants, and it is unclear how these dynamics play out in the networked, human-AI systems that increasingly shape cultural production. In this study, we analyze one such system: Artbreeder, which hosts daily “remix parties” in which users iteratively build on each other's work from a single seed image, producing branching lineages of images co-created by humans and generative AI. Using 130,882 images from 368 remix parties over 13 months, we find that images become less novel over the course of a party and that each remix step moves less far from its parents, consistent with the stabilization seen in iterated learning experiments, and that late-stage images drift toward the platform's dominant portrait style. More novel “parent” images produce more novel and more complex “children.” More novel children attract more likes but are not remixed more, whereas more complex children are remixed less. Finally, larger remix parties produce images that are more novel but less complex.

items.title: EBM-Nav: energy-based model for zero-shot visual navigation via implicit scene representation
items.abstract: Abstract Zero-shot visual navigation enables agents to generalize to unseen environments without task-specific training and is core to service robotics, warehouse logistics, and autonomous exploration. Existing approaches are observed to fail to achieve genuine zero-shot generalization: explicit-map methods rely on accurate reconstruction and are sensitive to sensor noise; supervised policies memorize training-scene patterns and degrade under illumination, furniture, and layout shifts; implicit representations offer continuous, differentiable encoding but remain confined to passive reconstruction and lack effective coupling with active decisions. To address this, EBM-Nav is proposed as a zero-shot navigation framework built on an energy-based model. Specifically, a periodic-activation implicit scene encoder is employed to map discrete RGB-D observations into a continuous, differentiable representation supporting arbitrary-resolution spatial queries. An energy function over the observation–action–goal triple is designed to reformulate navigation as gradient descent on an energy landscape. A frozen multimodal large language model is integrated to decompose long-horizon instructions into subgoals and generate candidate directions. A contrastive-divergence learning mechanism is developed with short-step Langevin dynamics to efficiently construct negative samples for training the energy function. Systematic experiments are conducted on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE continuous vision-and-language navigation benchmarks, and it is shown that EBM-Nav significantly outperforms state-of-the-art zero-shot methods in success rate, path efficiency, and navigation accuracy, while providing an interpretable energy-confidence mechanism for decisions. These results verify the energy-landscape zero-shot navigation paradigm, offer a general learning paradigm for embodied intelligence, and extend energy-based models from static perception to sequential decision-making, with methodological implications for service robots and autonomous exploration.

items.title: Effect of Trust in AI on Human AI Relationship among University Students
items.abstract: The study aimed to examine the effect of trust in AI on Human-AI relationship among university students. A cross-sectional survey research design was used. The sample comprised 300 university students (150 males and 150 females) selected through convenient sampling technique. Measures included the General Attitude toward AI Scale (GAAIS) by Schepman and Rodway (32 items, Positive α = .84, Negative α = .73), Short Trust in Automation Scale (S-TIAS) by McGrath et al. (3 items, α = .88), and Experiences in Human-AI Relationships Scale (EHARS) by Yang and Oshio (7 items). Correlation analysis showed that trust in AI was positively correlated with Human-AI relationship. The study contributed to the growing literature on Human-AI relationships by highlighting the role of trust in AI in Human-AI interactions among university students. The findings have important implications for AI literacy, technology acceptance, and the development of educational interventions aimed at fostering healthy and effective Human-AI relationships.

items.title: EFFECTS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) ON STUDENT PROBLEM-SOLVING SKILLS
items.abstract: This study determined the effect of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted pedagogy on the problem-solving skills of first-year Bachelor of Secondary Education students enrolled in Mathematics in the Modern World at Urdaneta City University. The study was completed in May 2026 during School Year 2025-2026. Using a quasi-experimental pre-test and post-test non-equivalent group design, the researchers compared the performance of students taught through conventional pedagogy with those who experienced AI-supported instruction. Problem-solving performance was examined using George Pólya's four-step framework: understanding the problem, planning a solution, carrying out the plan, and checking the solution. Initial results showed that both groups had limited problem-solving skills before instruction, especially in planning, execution, and verification. After the intervention, both groups improved; however, students exposed to AI-assisted pedagogy obtained stronger gains, particularly in carrying out the plan and overall problem-solving performance. The paired-samples t-test indicated significant improvement within the experimental group, while the independent-samples t-test showed that the experimental group outperformed the conventional group in selected post-test measures. The findings suggest that AI tools, when used with teacher guidance and structured problem-solving activities, can support mathematical learning by offering immediate feedback, alternative explanations, and opportunities for solution checking. The study further indicates that AI should be integrated as a cognitive support rather than as a substitute for independent reasoning.

items.title: Emerging paradigm in sensor based pedology: Advances, applications, challenges and future perspectives
items.abstract: Pedology has seen a significant revolution due to the adoption of modern sensors that can provide fast, non-invasive and high resolution measurements of soils. Traditional pedological surveys that rely on field work and laboratory analysis are efficient, yet time consuming, cumbersome and have exhibit low spatial resolution. Modern advancements in sensors that measure optical, geophysical, elemental, moisture and remote sensing characteristics of soils have considerably improved the evaluation of soil’s physical, chemical and morphological characteristics. This article provides a detailed overview of emerging sensor-based techniques in pedology including the principles of these techniques, their applications and limitations. The review further examines the roles of digital soil mapping (DSM), proximal soil sensing, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), machine learning and artificial intelligence in enhancing soil property prediction and spatial modelling. This review also highlights the significance of calibration and validation of sensors and ground truthing of observations. It critically analyses the problems associated with the calibration transferability, soil heterogeneity, moisture effects and cost of sensors. Recent advances in sensor fusion, internet of things (IoT)-enabled monitoring, hyperspectral imaging and explainable artificial intelligence are also discussed as promising directions for future soil assessment. Furthermore, major research gaps including the need for standardised calibration protocols, regional soil spectral libraries, affordable sensing technologies and interpretable machine-learning models are identified. Overall, sensor-based pedology complements conventional soil survey methods by providing accurate, efficient and spatially continuous soil information thereby supporting sustainable soil management, precision agriculture, environmental monitoring and evidence-based land-use planning under changing climatic conditions.

items.title: Emerging Technologies and Active Pedagogies in Initial Teacher Education: Preliminary Findings from a Systematic Review
items.abstract: Initial teacher education is under growing pressure to prepare future teachers for technology-rich classrooms and for pedagogical approaches that promote active student participation. This study presents preliminary findings from a systematic review examining how educational research addresses digital, emerging, and generative technologies in relation to the development of active pedagogies in initial teacher education. The review followed the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) protocol. Peer-reviewed articles published in English or Spanish between 2015 and June 2025 were retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, and Dialnet using three search strings related to new technologies, generative artificial intelligence, and active pedagogies in initial teacher education. Eligible studies focused on pre-service teachers and teacher educators in European and Latin American contexts. After full screening, 66 articles were included. Preliminary findings indicate that literature pays considerable attention to technology integration in school settings, whereas fewer studies examine how initial teacher education programs prepare pre-service teachers to implement innovative pedagogies supported by emerging technologies. These findings point to a persistent misalignment between teacher education, emerging technologies, and active pedagogies, as technology is often approached as a technical resource rather than as a driver of pedagogical transformation. The study offers an updated overview of research trends and identifies a persistent gap in the preparation of future teachers for innovative classroom practice.

items.title: Empathy as an Aesthetic Infrastructure of Intercultural Communication: China and Post-Yugoslav Digital Narratives in the Age of AI
items.abstract: This article examines intercultural communication between China and the post-Yugoslav states in the context of globalization and the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI), proposing empathy as a central yet ambivalent aesthetic infrastructure through which cultural difference is mediated. While digital platforms and AI technologies have dramatically increased the intensity and visibility of cross-cultural encounters, they have also transformed the conditions under which cultures are perceived, felt, and understood. Drawing on continental philosophy, moral psychology, and communication theory—particularly the work of Jean-Luc Nancy, Maurice Blanchot, Zygmunt Bauman, Martin Hoffman, and Jürgen Habermas—this study conceptualizes empathy not merely as a psychological or ethical capacity, but as an aesthetic and communicative form shaped by media technologies. Drawing on a theoretical-comparative and interpretative approach, the article examines Chinese and post-Yugoslav affective and aesthetic regimes as they are represented, circulated, and emotionally experienced within contemporary digital environments. Chinese culture is globally circulated through narratives of harmony, technological progress, and collective futurity, while post-Yugoslav cultures are framed through trauma, nostalgia, and emotional authenticity. These representations invite empathic engagement, yet often at the cost of historical depth, internal plurality, and ethical responsibility. The article argues that AI-driven empathy produces emotional proximity without genuine dialogue, replacing communicative understanding with affective optimization. In response, it proposes a critical aesthetics of empathic communication that preserves distance, opacity, and interpretive labor as necessary conditions for meaningful intercultural dialogue. Such an approach is essential for rethinking cultural exchange between China and the post-Yugoslav space in the age of artificial intelligence.

items.title: Energy Audits in Tanzanian Industrial SMEs for Methods, Barriers, and M&V-Linked Savings Prioritization
items.abstract: This chapter develops a conceptual and methodological framework for artificial-intelligence- and machine-learning-enabled energy audits in Tanzanian industrial small and medium-sized enterprises. Industrial SMEs often face energy-efficiency barriers related to limited capital, weak information systems, incomplete metering, and constrained managerial capacity. The chapter positions the energy audit as the organizing mechanism for sustainable energy engineering and shows how AI/ML can strengthen load profiling, benchmarking, anomaly detection, forecasting, measure prioritization, and measurement and verification. Drawing on peer-reviewed evidence from SME audit programs, ISO 50001 research, African industrial energy studies, and applied AI/ML energy literature, the chapter proposes a staged implementation roadmap for Tanzanian SMEs. The contribution is a practical pathway for moving from one-off audits toward data-informed, explainable, and financially grounded energy management.

items.title: Energy Forecasting and Prediction Using Intelligent Controllers: AI-Driven Strategies for Microgrid Optimization
items.abstract: In this chapter, we introduce a solar irradiance prediction and forecasting method for microgrid optimization based on artificial intelligence (AI), which employs Global Tilted Irradiance (GTI) as a key input to improve the accuracy of photovoltaic (PV) power prediction. Unlike conventional irradiance indices, GTI aligns better with real-world setups, particularly due to its relevance for tilted solar panels. Based on historical data from Visakhapatnam, India, three machine learning models Random Forest, XGBoost, and CatBoost were trained to predict GTI. CatBoost delivered the most accurate results, having the highest R 2 (0.9993) and lowest Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) (7.37). Furthermore, CatBoost was used to forecast GTI values that were connected to operational decision-making in batteries, loads, and grid interaction. These strategies were implemented in an Energy Management System (EMS) for automated control. The study demonstrates how GTI-based forecasting with intelligent controllers enhances microgrid performance, reliability, and sustainability.

items.title: Enhancing Democratic Listening in Online Discussions: The Role of Reaction Buttons, Discussion Moderation, and Large Language Models
items.abstract: Political communication research in general – and research on political online discussions in particular – has previously focused on the exercise of democratic voice and thus largely neglected the complementary practice of democratic listening. Against the backdrop of a wide-spread perception that democratic listening is lacking in online discussions, we investigate whether listening can be strengthened through novel platform affordances. We developed an experimental online written discussion platform with listening-oriented reaction buttons and both human and AI moderation (based on GPT-4). We then conducted an experiment involving n = 740 respondents in 40 discussion groups (N = 4,355 comments), each lasting 30 minutes, covering three experimental conditions and a control condition. We compare the effect of (1) listening-oriented reaction buttons versus (2) a combination of these buttons and listening-oriented human discussion moderation versus (3) a combination of buttons and AI moderation on the level of democratic listening demonstrated in discussants’ textual contributions. We find that listening-oriented buttons alone do not enhance democratic listening. However, when combined with listening-oriented AI moderation, they are associated with a democratic listening rate of 27% within discussions, compared to 21% in the condition without either feature. Our findings lay the basis for the implementation of a combination of listening-oriented buttons and discussion moderation on news media websites, social media apps or dedicated discussion spaces using LLM-based chatbots.

items.title: Enhancing Empathy in Nursing Students Through a Multimodal Artificial Intelligence-Supported Simulation: A Mixed-Methods Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Empathic communication is a core competency in nursing practice, yet providing nursing students with realistic opportunities to develop this competency remains challenging. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have enabled the integration of behavioral and physiological data into simulation-based education. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effectiveness of a multimodal AI-supported simulation in improving empathy, communication self-efficacy, and learning engagement among undergraduate nursing students. METHODS: A quasi-experimental pretest-posttest study was conducted with 134 undergraduate nursing students (68 experimental and 66 control). The experimental group received multimodal AI-supported simulation integrating conversational AI, facial emotion recognition, speech analysis, and physiological monitoring, whereas the control group received conventional role-play-based simulation with faculty-led debriefing. RESULTS: After adjustment for baseline scores, the experimental group showed significantly greater improvements in empathy, communication self-efficacy, and emotional, behavioral, and cognitive engagement than the control group (all P < .001). Heart rate variability and galvanic skin response showed significant group-by-time differences, indicating differential physiological responses during the simulation. Qualitative findings indicated enhanced empathy awareness, communication confidence, and reflective learning. items.title: Enhancing Large Language Models with External Knowledge Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Critical Review of Retrieval Design, Context Compression, Safety and Evaluation, with a Conceptual Governance-Aware Architecture
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) depend on static parametric knowledge, leading to outdated answers, missing expertise, and hallucinations. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses these issues by retrieving external evidence during inference, but the interactions between design choices are not well understood. This critical review explores configuration benchmarking, embedding quality, question-type-adaptive retrieval with context compression, comparison with fine-tuning, IAM-based permission filtering, and real-time, safety-critical graph-based RAG. A focused narrative design was used on a defined corpus, with foundational sources. The findings show that no single RAG configuration is best, as the optimal choice depends on the task and metrics. Retrieval quality strongly correlates with answer quality for extractive tasks but weakly for synthesis tasks. Adaptive retrieval and compression can reduce token usage but increase latency. Access control, freshness, and safety can be enforced outside the LLM, but this is only possible under explicit trust assumptions. However, most studies rely on Wikipedia-based question answering, small samples, single runs, and inconsistent metrics. Several studies also contain internal inconsistencies, which are documented here. This review contributes five key elements: a survey matrix, a comparative analysis that separates different experimental settings, an eight-layer conceptual architecture justified by literature, a minimum evaluation protocol for fair comparison, and a research gap agenda linked to evidence. These outputs provide researchers and practitioners with a foundation for building reliable, secure, and governable RAG systems in real-world, enterprise, and safety-critical applications.

items.title: Estereotipos Algorítmicos: Un Estudio Experimental sobre Sesgos de Género en la IA Generative
items.abstract: This study analyzes how citizens identify gender biases in narratives generated by artificial intelligence (AI), using ChatGPT as a case study. An online experiment was conducted with 614 Spanish participants, randomly assigned to three conditions: a professional success narrative featuring a female protagonist, a narrative featuring a male protagonist, and a neutral narrative. After exposure, gender bias detection in the story, perceived bias in ChatGPT, and the intention to reduce or correct algorithmic biases were measured. The results show that the narrative featuring a female protagonist was associated with higher bias detection and greater attribution of partiality to ChatGPT. No significant differences were observed according to participants’ gender or educational level. Likewise, indicators of proximity to AI, such as interest in these technologies and the use of AI-based applications, were associated with lower perceived bias in the tool. The findings underscore the need to promote critical AI literacy that helps citizens more critically recognize when its outputs reproduce gender stereotypes or inequalities.

items.title: Ethical and Legal Dimensions of AI in Digital Forensics and Cybersecurity
items.abstract: The use of technology to gather, store, examine, and display digital evidence in accordance with a set of regulations is known as digital forensics. According to Cyber, the variety of cyberattitudes is altering people’s perceptions of cybercrime in a distinctive manner. This facilitates the acquisition of digital evidence and the handling of digital content. Due to the increasing prevalence of cyber dangers in the digital environment, “manual” forensic investigations are rapidly becoming obsolete. Most people whose job it is to locate digital evidence have recently been affected by this critical predicament. It cannot advance by using fresh strategies and tactics. To address this demand, it must develop new methods and instruments as fast and precisely as it did before. Artificial intelligence, deep learning, machine learning, and the development of natural human language have all contributed to significant change. Every cybersecurity and digital forensics specialist in the world might benefit from these new tools and systems, which could also alter how they do their duties.

items.title: Ethical Considerations in AI-Driven Travel Management Systems
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into travel management systems presents profound ethical challenges that demand systematic examination. This chapter investigates the multifaceted ethical dimensions arising from AI deployment in travel management, encompassing algorithmic bias, data privacy, transparency, human agency, environmental sustainability, and equity of access. Drawing on recent scholarship in AI ethics, information systems, and tourism studies, the chapter argues that uncritical adoption of AI in travel management risks entrenching discrimination, eroding traveller autonomy, and exacerbating socioeconomic divides. The chapter proposes a normative framework grounded in fairness, accountability, and sustainability principles to guide responsible AI deployment. Recommendations for practitioners, policymakers, and technology developers are provided to ensure that AI-driven travel systems serve human flourishing and inclusive progress.

items.title: Evaluating Locally Grounded Generative AI for Health-Policy Support: A Multilevel Mixed-Methods Pilot Study
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may assist evidence-informed health-policy work, but favorable user perceptions and well-written outputs do not establish factual reliability or implementation readiness. A multilevel mixed-methods pilot evaluation examined MUSYA AI, a locally grounded policy-support platform in Thailand. Thirty-five health-sector personnel completed questionnaires, seven participated in Think-Aloud observation, sixteen Policy Briefs were assessed using an expert rubric, and seventy factual claims underwent evidence auditing. The document comparison included eight MUSYA AI and eight ChatGPT (GPT-5.6, OpenAI) outputs under common task instructions and system-specific information access. Mean System Usability Scale, perceived usefulness, and trust scores were 97.29/100, 4.70/5, and 4.57/5, respectively. Ceiling effects and limited internal consistency constrained interpretation of these descriptive indices; user experience, ease of use, and behavioral intention were interpreted at the item level. Observations documented reading and editing, but successful error detection and correction were not evaluated. MUSYA AI documents received higher overall quality ratings than comparator documents (95.38 ± 2.39 versus 72.25 ± 11.90; difference, 23.13 points; bootstrap 95% confidence interval, 15.63–31.38; Hedges’ g = 2.55). However, classification–rationale inconsistencies affected forty-five claims (64.3%), leaving comparative factual-accuracy findings provisional. The small, nonrandomized document sample and absence of verified task pairing prevented causal attribution of quality differences. MUSYA AI elicited favorable pilot-user perceptions and produced higher-rated documents within the evaluated sample. These findings support continued supervised evaluation; institutional readiness requires traceable claim adjudication, demonstrated oversight effectiveness, and broader controlled assessment.

items.title: Evaluating the effectiveness of AI-Based adaptive learning for reading development and self-regulated learning among pupils with dyslexia in Abuja, Nigeria
items.abstract: Children with dyslexia often experience persistent challenges in reading, motivation, and self-regulation within traditional classroom settings that rely on uniform instructional approaches. With the growing integration of artificial intelligence in education, AI-based adaptive learning systems have emerged as innovative tools capable of personalizing instruction and supporting diverse learning needs. This study investigated the effect of AI-based adaptive learning systems on reading performance, motivation, and self-regulation among primary school students with dyslexia in Abuja, Nigeria. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control group design was adopted, with a sample of 60 Primary 5 pupils drawn from selected inclusive and special education schools in the Abuja Municipal Area. Data were collected using a Reading Performance Test, Motivation toward Reading Scale, and Self-Regulation in Reading Questionnaire, and analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, including independent samples t-test. Findings revealed that students exposed to AI-based adaptive learning demonstrated significantly higher improvements across all variables compared to those receiving conventional instruction. The experimental group recorded substantial gains in reading performance (mean gain = 24.20), motivation (mean gain = 1.50), and self-regulation (mean gain = 1.60), compared to the control group. Statistical analysis confirmed that these differences were significant (p < 0.05). These findings align with Cognitive Load Theory, Self-Determination Theory, and Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development. The study concludes that AI-based adaptive learning systems offer an effective approach for improving both academic and psychological outcomes among students with dyslexia. It recommends the integration of AI-driven instructional tools in primary education, alongside teacher training and policy support, to promote inclusive, personalized, and effective learning environments.

items.title: EVALUATION OF INTERNAL CONTROLS OVER THE REVENUE CYCLE: A CASE STUDY OF RETAIL COMPANY X
items.abstract: This study evaluates internal controls over the revenue cycle at Retail X, a modern convenience store chain operating a digital ordering application integrated with a Point of Sale (POS) system. The evaluation applies the COSO Internal Control–Integrated Framework/ICIF (COSO, 2013), focusing on two components: Risk Assessment and Control Activities. A descriptive case study approach was employed, with data collected through semi-structured interviews with three informants—the Store Manager, Cashier, and Service Crew—and analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings identify four operational risks: transaction input errors, product preparation errors, order pickup errors, and disruptions in receiving digital orders. These risks stem from employee-customer-system interactions and limitations in human resources and digital infrastructure. Control activities implemented include order confirmation, preparation SOPs, order labeling, product remaking, and manual order verification. However, the evaluation reveals uneven control coverage, heavy reliance on human factors, and a predominance of corrective over preventive controls. By tracing risk from its source to the adequacy of existing controls, this study extends the application of COSO ICIF to digitally integrated retail settings in developing economies. The study concludes that strengthening internal control requires procedural improvements alongside enhanced human resource capacity and information system infrastructure.

items.title: Evidence-Grounded Autonomous Web Application Testing: A Scope-Aware Framework for Reliable AI-Generated QA Reports
items.abstract: Abstract Autonomous artificial intelligence agents powered by large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for web application testing, usability evaluation, and software quality assurance. However, significant challenges remain in ensuring reliable defect detection, comprehensive test coverage, reproducible findings, and evidence-based reporting. This working paper introduces Evidence-Grounded Autonomous Quality Assurance (EG-AQA), a proposed framework for improving the transparency, reliability, and reproducibility of AI-generated web application testing reports. The framework combines task-oriented browser exploration, structured evidence collection, independent verification mechanisms, explicit testing-scope accounting, and uncertainty-aware reporting. The research examines how autonomous testing systems can distinguish verified software defects from unsupported interpretations, incomplete observations, environmental restrictions, and issues requiring human judgment. It also proposes quantitative evaluation methods for measuring defect-detection precision and recall, navigation coverage, task completion, finding reproducibility, and computational efficiency. The study uses an anonymized, limited observation from an early-stage Cohorvix testing report to illustrate challenges associated with incomplete exploration and the interpretation of automated testing evidence. A reproducible experimental methodology is proposed for future validation using controlled web applications, independently documented defects, repeated testing sessions, comparative baselines, and human adjudication. The paper contributes a structured research framework and evaluation protocol intended to support more accountable and evidence-grounded AI-powered website testing. The proposed improvements have not yet been validated through a completed comparative experiment. Publication status: Research working paper, Version 1.0. items.abstract: Conspectus As one of the most formidable threats to human health, cancer demands technologies that can sensitively detect malignancies, precisely guide intervention, adapt to dynamic disease states, and support clinical decision-making. Phototheranostics based on organic fluorophores have shown great promise in cancer management owing to their tunable structural design, tumor-targeting capability, real-time imaging output, and biocompatibility with diverse therapeutic modalities. However, conventional fluorophores often suffer from aggregation-caused quenching in concentrated or biological aggregate states, leading to weakened signals, insufficient sensitivity, and limited therapeutic efficacy. The discovery of aggregation-induced emission (AIE) provides a conceptually distinct solution to this problem. AIE materials are weakly emissive in the molecularly dispersed state but become highly luminescent upon aggregation, thereby turning aggregation from a detrimental process into a useful photophysical mechanism. By precisely controlling molecular motion, AIE materials can exhibit advantages including high signal-to-noise ratio, large Stokes shifts, and excellent photostability, making them a versatile molecular toolbox for tumor-oriented phototheranostic systems. Over the past two decades, they have evolved beyond simple fluorescent probes into integrated platforms for cancer theranostics. In this Account, we propose a concept-driven framework, termed AIMS (Analyze-Intervene-Modulate-Select), to organize the evolution of AIE materials in cancer diagnosis and therapy according to their distinctive roles within cancer management. The first generation, “Analyze”, refers to AIE materials used mainly as diagnostic tools. These systems enable sensitive detection of tumor-associated biomarkers, in vivo lesion visualization, and multimodal intraoperative identification. The second generation, “Intervene”, generates all-in-one theranostic platforms that couple imaging with phototherapy, facilitating radiotherapy sensitization, immune activation, or postoperative control. The third generation, “Modulate”, describes intelligent and adaptive AIE platforms that respond to therapy-induced stress, microenvironmental shifts, or dynamic biological feedback during treatment, transforming static theranostics into systems capable of modulating therapeutic trajectories. The emerging fourth generation, “Select”, represents a data-driven paradigm linking the design of AIE materials with artificial intelligence, multiomics, patient stratification, model selection, and indication prioritization. Through AIMS, we organize the accumulated capabilities of AIE materials around four functional roles. By clarifying which role is most relevant to a given application, AIMS guides future research in prioritizing design objectives, integrating the functions needed for the intended task, and matching material innovation to specific needs in cancer management.

In the context of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, the proceedings provide a forum for academic exchange on approaches intended to make teaching and learning more participatory, accessible, and responsive to diverse learners, including learners with disabilities. items.title: Explainable AI and Real-Time Decisioning for Automated Government Case Management in Saudi Arabia
items.abstract: Automated government case management is moving from digitised workflow toward intelligent triage, eligibility assessment, risk prioritisation and service routing. In Saudi Arabia, this transition is especially consequential because digital government programmes increasingly connect high-volume public services with data-intensive decision processes. The central challenge is not simply whether artificial intelligence can accelerate case handling, but whether decisions can remain timely, reviewable, understandable and contestable when models operate at operational speed. This review examines how explainable artificial intelligence and real-time decisioning can be combined for automated government case management in Saudi Arabia. It synthesises thirty DOI-verified studies published from 2020 to 2025 across explainability, human-AI decision support, public-sector algorithmic governance, Saudi digital government and streaming analytics. The review develops a socio-technical framework in which case intake, data quality, machine reasoning, rule validation, explanation generation, human oversight, notification, appeal and continuous monitoring form one auditable decision loop. The analysis finds that explainability is valuable only when it is matched to the decision recipient and linked to operational controls; generic feature-attribution displays alone do not guarantee justified or trustworthy outcomes. Real-time systems also require explicit latency budgets, uncertainty handling, concept-drift monitoring and escalation rules so that speed does not suppress due process. For Saudi public agencies, successful adoption depends on combining interoperable data, secure governance, accountable ownership and Arabic-capable explanation interfaces with measurable human override and appeal mechanisms. The study proposes evaluation criteria spanning predictive validity, explanation fidelity, decision latency, fairness, reviewability and institutional accountability. It concludes that explainable real-time case management should be designed as governed decision infrastructure rather than as an isolated prediction model.

items.title: Explainable AI in Neural Poetry Generation: Beyond Attention
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is increasingly important for ensuring transparency and trust in neural systems; however, its applicability to creative text generation remains limited. Neural poetry generation models produce linguistically coherent and stylistically rich outputs, yet explaining decisions such as metaphor construction, emotional tone, and thematic development remains unresolved. This systematic literature review synthesizes 26 peer‐reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2026, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and a predefined protocol across four major digital libraries. The analysis identifies a fundamental mismatch between existing XAI paradigms and the properties of generative modeling. We propose a taxonomy distinguishing classification‐native methods from generation‐compatible approaches, highlighting their differing assumptions. Based on established criteria of contrastivity, selectivity, and faithfulness, we show that attention mechanisms lack causal validity as explanatory tools. To consolidate these findings, we introduce a unified failure framework comprising five interacting structural limitations: token–semantic mismatch, attention non‐causality, classification–generation incompatibility, evaluation collapse, and human–model ontological misalignment. These limitations collectively constrain the effectiveness of current XAI methods in creative contexts. Our findings indicate that advancing explainability in neural poetry generation requires a shift toward semantic‐level representations, causal intervention‐based approaches, and human‐centered evaluation frameworks that incorporate aesthetic and interpretive dimensions.

items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Improving Transparency and Reliability in Automated Decision-Making Systems
items.abstract: Automated decision-making systems increasingly influence healthcare, finance, recruitment, education, public administration, and digital platforms. Although advanced machine-learning models can discover complex relationships, their opaque reasoning can obstruct auditing, contestability, and safe deployment. This narrative review examines how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) may improve transparency and reliability by clarifying model behavior, revealing data dependencies, supporting error detection, and enabling informed human oversight. It synthesizes established work on interpretable modeling, local feature attribution, surrogate explanations, counterfactual reasoning, explanation evaluation, and governance. A conceptual assurance framework connects data provenance, predictive validation, explanation fidelity, subgroup analysis, and operational monitoring. The paper distinguishes understandable explanations from evidence that a system is accurate, robust, or fair: an attractive explanation alone does not establish reliability. A non-empirical diagram illustrates complementary assurance dimensions without implying measured results. Practical implications include tailoring explanations to decision recipients, testing explanation stability under perturbations, documenting uncertainty, and establishing appeal mechanisms. The review concludes that XAI is most effective when embedded within a wider socio-technical accountability process rather than deployed as a stand-alone visualization technique.

items.title: Explainable CatBoost–TabPFN Hybrid for Mode-Resolved Interlaminar Fracture Toughness Prediction in Fiber-Reinforced Polymer Composites
items.abstract: Fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP) composites offer high specific strength, high stiffness, and good corrosion resistance, which makes them suitable for aerospace, automotive, marine, and wind-energy structures. Their interlaminar fracture behavior is harder to pin down because delamination testing is slow and costly and the response shifts with loading mode. This study presents an explainable hybrid machine learning framework for interlaminar fracture toughness under Mode-I, Mode-II, and Mixed-Mode loading. A weighted ensemble pairs Categorical Boosting (CatBoost), a gradient-boosting method, with the Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN), a pretrained transformer built for tabular data. A Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) tunes the CatBoost hyperparameters and the ensemble weight against specimen-grouped cross-validation. The work draws on the public D-STANDART experimental dataset and treats DCB, ELS, and MMB as three separate prediction problems for GIC, GIIC, and GC rather than pooling them into one model. The analyzed D-STANDART specimens comprise pultruded carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) material based on Zoltek PX35 carbon fiber. The data are partitioned at the specimen level, so no specimen contributes records to more than one subset, and feature selection uses the training data alone. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) then measure how each input shifts the predicted toughness in each mode. The framework reached an R2 of 0.9280 for DCB, 0.9870 for ELS, and 0.9627 for MMB, with RMSE values of 5.1759, 1.5041, and 2.8809 and MAE values of 1.6502, 0.5372, and 0.7000, respectively. Bringing a tabular foundation model into delamination analysis, and keeping the three loading modes apart, lets the framework report mode-specific feature behavior instead of one averaged picture.

items.title: Exploring Mongolian Trilingual Students’ Perceptions About Academic and Affective Impacts of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Technologies: A Descriptive Qualitative Study
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into education has received increasing attention over the past couple of years. However, the perceived impacts of such technologies by trilingual learners have remained unaddressed by scholars. Compared with conventional second or foreign language learners, trilingual learners may need to coordinate languages with different levels of proficiency and functions while also coping with unequal AI support across languages. To fill the gap, this descriptive qualitative study drew on technology acceptance model (TAM) and control‐value theory (CVT) to examine Mongolian trilingual learners’ perceptions about the academic and affective impacts of AI tools. A sample of 40 Mongolian trilingual students in Inner Mongolia, China were asked to complete an open‐ended questionnaire and attend an interview. The results of thematic analysis demonstrated that AI technologies had imposed several positive and negative academic and affective impacts on trilingual students. Particularly, it was found that AI adoption could improve learning efficiency, autonomy, and agency, but over‐reliance on AI tools might lead to dependency, plagiarism acts, surface learning, and reduced critical thinking. Regarding affective consequences, the students found AI adoption exciting, motivating, and emotionally safe, while they endorsed the possibility of anxiety, stress, fear, emotional tension, and emotional detachment. The study discusses the findings and provides practical implications for trilingual teachers, students, and policymakers by enhancing their AI and emotional literacy.

items.title: EXPRESS: From Chit-Chat to Conversion: Cost-Efficient Conversational Recommendation via Retrospective Learning and Isolated Reflection
items.abstract: Conversational recommendation systems help digital platforms elicit user preferences through multi-turn interaction, but they often face a practical tension between recommendation accuracy and interaction cost when users provide vague or low-information inputs. This study follows a design science approach to develop a cost-conscious conversational recommendation artifact for such ambiguous service encounters. The artifact is guided by two design principles. First, retrospective outcome-guided supervision uses successful historical conversion trajectories as downstream anchors for improving responses at earlier low-information states. Second, isolated reflection separates recommendation generation from consistency checking, enabling diagnostic regeneration when candidate responses conflict with previously stated user constraints. In implementation, the artifact instantiates these principles through parameter-efficient adaptation of open-source large language models and prompt-isolated role switching over a shared backbone model. We validate the artifact on three conversational recommendation datasets covering movie and e-commerce settings, using outcome efficacy, interaction efficiency, process analysis, ablation analysis, robustness checks, and human evaluation. Here, interaction efficiency refers to user-visible dialogue turns, while computational burden is reported separately through training, memory, and latency measurements. The empirical results show that the artifact improves recommendation effectiveness while maintaining a favorable balance between interaction burden and conversion outcomes under the tested conditions. Process-level analysis further characterizes how recommendation behavior evolves over the course of dialogue. This study contributes transferable design principles for embedding retrospective preference optimization and isolated reflection into conversational recommendation systems, offering operational guidance for platforms seeking to improve personalization under constraints on interaction cost.

items.title: Factors influencing registered nurses’ attitudes toward and literacy in artificial intelligence: a cross-sectional systematic review
items.abstract: Background Presently, artificial intelligence technology is being extensively applied across clinical nursing practice. However, whether this technology can be deeply integrated into clinical workflows depends largely on nurses’ attitudes and literacy regarding artificial intelligence. Consequently, conducting an in depth exploration of core factors shaping registered nurses’ artificial intelligence attitudes and literacy holds significant importance for driving the rapid development of intelligent nursing. Methods This study strictly adhered to PRISMA guidelines. Systematic searches were conducted across seven English databases, namely PubMed, Web of Science, Medline, Embase, The Cochrane Library, IEEE Xplore, and CINAHL, alongside three Chinese databases, including China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang Data, and VIP Database. The search timeframe ranged from database inception through May 30, 2026. Following screening according to inclusion and exclusion criteria, independent factors influencing attitudes and literacy were extracted. Employing a narrative synthesis approach, these influencing factors were categorized, summarized, and narratively integrated across distinct thematic domains. Results A total of 30 studies involving 12,958 registered nurses were included in this systematic review. The majority of the studies were conducted in China and Turkey. The independent factors influencing registered nurses’ attitudes toward artificial intelligence included educational attainment, age, length of service, gender, professional title/nursing level, hospital tier/category, AI awareness/understanding/knowledge, AI training experience, AI usage experience, artificial intelligence anxiety, and digital leadership. The factors independently affecting nurses’ artificial intelligence literacy included leadership style, AI training experience, and usage experience/frequency. Conclusion Current evidence indicates that key modifiable factors to improve nurses’ attitudes toward and literacy in artificial intelligence include AI-related training, practical hands-on experience, and organizational leadership, while technical anxiety should not be overlooked. Compared with demographic characteristics, educational and experiential interventions appear more effective in enhancing nurses’ artificial intelligence literacy levels. Nursing managers should actively implement smart training programs, increase opportunities for nurses to apply new technologies in clinical practice, and formulate relevant policies regarding data privacy protection and accountability division, thereby promoting the safe and effective integration of AI technology into patient care. items.title: Fear-Specific Technophobia as a Mediator Between Daily Technical Support and Instrumental Versus Hedonic Technology Use in Later Life: Cross-Sectional Survey Study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Population aging and rapid digitalization have intensified concerns about older adults’ digital participation. Although access disparities have narrowed, older adults continue to differ from younger groups in how they use digital technologies, with their use skewed toward instrumental rather than hedonic purposes. Technophobia is a salient psychological barrier; yet, its distinct fear dimensions and their links to different forms of technology use remain insufficiently differentiated. Daily technical support (DTS) may provide an important sociotechnical context for understanding these relationships. Objective This study aimed to test how DTS promotes older adults’ instrumental and hedonic technology use by reducing multidimensional technophobia (fear of inconvenience, fear of personal failure, and human-machine ambiguity) and whether these mechanisms differ by gender. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among Chinese adults aged ≥55 years recruited via online platforms and offline communities in Nanjing (June-October 2024). A total of 212 valid responses were included (mean age 66.96, SD 6.96, range 55‐86 years; 142/212, 68.4% women). Measures assessed day-to-day technical support, 3 dimensions of technophobia, instrumental versus hedonic technology use, and demographic variables. We used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5000 bootstrap resamples to test direct, indirect, and moderated mediation effects, reporting 95% bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) CI. Results DTS significantly reduced fear of inconvenience (β=−0.455, 95% BCa CI −0.632 to −0.229; P <.001) but did not significantly affect fear of personal failure ( P =.12) or human-machine ambiguity ( P =.26). Fear of inconvenience and human-machine ambiguity negatively predicted instrumental use (IU; β=−0.215, 95% BCa CI −0.410 to −0.009; P =.05 and β=−0.211, 95% BCa CI −0.389 to −0.001; P =.04). DTS had a positive direct effect on IU (β=0.104, 95% BCa CI 0.009 to 0.203; P =.04) but not on hedonic use (HU; β=0.075; P =.11). The indirect effect of DTS on IU through fear of inconvenience was significant (β=0.097, 95% BCa CI 0.020-0.204). Gender moderated the effect of DTS on fear of inconvenience (β=0.287, 95% BCa CI 0.052-0.518; P =.02), and such conditional indirect effect was significant for men (β=0.098, 95% BCa CI 0.001-0.219) but not for women (β=0.036, 95% BCa CI −0.002 to 0.116). Conclusions DTS was associated with greater instrumental technology use among older adults through lower fear of inconvenience, with a stronger indirect association among men, whereas no comparable pathway emerged for HU. This suggests that gender may shape how older adults benefit psychologically from technical support rather than reflect general differences in support needs. Interventions should move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches by providing targeted, task-oriented support that addresses older adults’ specific technological fears and practical barriers.
